strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored problem: neural surrogate modeling of compressible, shock-containing flows on nonuniform temporal grids.

ShockCast is conceptually clear, combining learned timestep selection with a timestep-conditioned neural solver. The gradient/CFL features, Euler residual conditioning, and timestep-gated mixture-of-experts variants are physically motivated.
The authors contribute two challenging 2D datasets, including a multiphase coal-dust setting, and provide substantial CFD-generation and training details.

The experiments cover four established solver backbones, multiple conditioning schemes, three training runs, autoregressive evaluation, and several flow-oriented metrics. The appendices contain useful quantitative tables and qualitative field visualizations.
The paper is generally well organized and includes appropriate discussion of long-horizon reliability and potential dual-use applications.
weaknesses: The central claim that adaptive time-stepping is beneficial is not directly evaluated. There is no fixed/uniform-timestep neural-solver baseline, nor an accuracy-versus-number-of-steps or accuracy-versus-runtime comparison. Thus, the results establish that the proposed pipeline can operate on adaptively sampled data, but not that it improves accuracy or computational efficiency relative to simpler alternatives.

The two phases are not adequately disentangled. Missing comparisons include a solver supplied with oracle ground-truth timesteps, a solver using a constant or heuristic timestep, and the complete system using alternative timestep predictors. Consequently, it is unclear how much error comes from timestep prediction versus state evolution and whether the neural CFL module is necessary.

The neural CFL evaluation is weak: it reports normalized one-step MAE and only a single selected unrolled trajectory per dataset. Aggregate rollout errors, time-drift or stopping-time errors, failure rates, and sensitivity to biased timestep predictions are absent.

Despite motivating the work through computational savings, the paper reports no end-to-end inference time or speedup against the CFD solver, and no comparison at matched accuracy or computational budget. Model FLOPs alone do not support the practical acceleration claim.

The physical validation is incomplete for shock-dominated compressible flow. There are no conservation errors, shock-location/strength errors, stability statistics, or checks for unphysical states. Pearson correlation and global mean-flow/TKE metrics may hide local errors at discontinuities; some coal-dust rollout errors are also large, such as roughly 43–45% for transverse velocity.

The empirical improvements from the proposed Euler and MoE conditioning mechanisms are inconsistent and often negligible or negative relative to the existing base conditioning. The paper does not provide a convincing aggregate analysis demonstrating that these new mechanisms outperform standard timestep conditioning.

Generalization evidence is narrow: only two 2D configurations from the same CFD code are considered, with small evaluation sets of 9–10 cases. The split construction is insufficiently specified, and there are no out-of-range parameter tests, different geometries/boundaries, resolution-transfer tests, or genuinely hypersonic cases.

The broad novelty statements, including being the first framework for learning high-speed flows, are stronger than the evidence and positioning support. The technically defensible novelty is narrower: learned temporal adaptation for these high-speed-flow surrogate settings.

Although reproducibility details are substantial, important items remain unclear, including precise parameter sampling and train/test split rules, normalization, rollout termination when a predicted step crosses the final time, and complete neural-CFL architecture details. Overall, the missing baselines leave the paper's main adaptive-time-stepping contribution unsupported at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: learned surrogate modeling of compressible, shock-containing flows on adaptive temporal meshes.
ShockCast is conceptually simple and clearly presented, separating timestep prediction from timestep-conditioned state evolution.
The two generated datasets include nontrivial supersonic dynamics, including multiphase shock interaction and reflected circular shocks.
The experiments cover four neural-solver backbones, multiple conditioning mechanisms, three training runs, rollout metrics, physical summary quantities, and detailed computational statistics.
The appendix provides useful implementation, dataset-generation, visualization, and broader-impact information.
weaknesses: The central claim that learned adaptive time-stepping is beneficial is not demonstrated. There is no uniform-timestep baseline, fixed-step model with matched compute, direct next-snapshot predictor without timestep conditioning, or comparison of accuracy versus the number of model evaluations.

The two-phase design is insufficiently validated. Oracle ground-truth timestep conditioning is missing, so errors from timestep prediction and state evolution cannot be separated; there is also no ablation replacing the neural CFL module with a simple analytic, statistical, or persistence predictor.

The proposed conditioning mechanisms provide weak and inconsistent gains. Euler and MoE conditioning are frequently indistinguishable from or worse than the base conditioning, and the strongest model depends on the metric and dataset.

The neural CFL model merely imitates the coarsened timestep schedule of one CFD solver. It neither enforces the CFL condition nor learns an accuracy-cost policy, and the paper provides no stability, conservation, or error-control guarantee.

Evaluation is restricted to two closely related synthetic two-dimensional datasets with only 9 or 10 held-out parameter cases. There are no out-of-distribution tests over Mach number, geometry, boundary conditions, spatial resolution, temporal coarsening, or longer rollout horizons.
Important prior adaptive-time approaches discussed in the related-work section are not included as empirical baselines, making the novelty and comparative effectiveness difficult to assess.

Rollout predictions are linearly interpolated onto the reference temporal grid before several metrics are computed. This can obscure accumulated timing error, yet direct trajectory-time errors, stopping-time errors, and sensitivity to interpolation are not reported.

Despite motivating the work through computational acceleration, the paper reports neither wall-clock inference speed nor end-to-end speedup against the CFD solver, and it does not evaluate accuracy at matched computational cost.

The models do not enforce conservation laws, positivity, shock conditions, or other physical constraints. Large errors remain for challenging quantities, such as approximately 42–46% unrolled error for the coal-dust y-velocity, without adequate analysis.

Overall, the datasets and engineering effort are useful, but the current experimental design cannot establish that adaptive learned stepping—or the proposed additions specifically—improves over simpler alternatives. This is a major evidentiary gap for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and relatively underexplored problem: learned surrogate modeling of compressible, shock-dominated flows on adaptive temporal grids.

ShockCast is conceptually clear: one network predicts the next timestep and a timestep-conditioned neural solver advances the state. The physically motivated timestep features, Euler-residual conditioning, and timestep-gated mixture-of-experts variants are sensible.
The evaluation covers two newly generated and substantially different datasets, including a challenging multiphase coal-dust setting, and examines four established solver backbones.

The experiments report three-run uncertainty estimates, one-step and autoregressive errors, correlation time, mean-flow error, and turbulent kinetic energy error. Detailed solver, training, computational-cost, and dataset-generation information improves reproducibility.

Qualitative rollouts and timestep trajectories show that the framework can track adaptive temporal grids and reproduce important flow structures. The broader-impact discussion appropriately acknowledges reliability and dual-use concerns.
weaknesses: The central motivation—that learned adaptive stepping is preferable to uniform stepping—is not directly tested. A fixed-timestep baseline matched for either computational budget or accuracy is essential, as is an oracle-timestep ablation separating timestep-prediction error from state-evolution error.

The paper does not report end-to-end wall-clock speedups, numbers of learned rollout steps, or accuracy-versus-cost curves relative to the CFD solver. Consequently, the claimed computational benefit remains largely prospective.

The proposed Euler and MoE conditioning mechanisms provide inconsistent and usually small gains over the existing base conditioning. In many table entries the base method is competitive or superior, so the evidence for these methodological contributions is weak.

Neural-CFL evaluation is limited: normalized MAE and a single example trajectory do not establish robustness. Results should include relative or physical-unit errors across all test cases, accumulated timing drift, failure rates, and comparisons with simple predictors or available coarse-grid CFL estimates.

Performance on the more challenging coal-dust dataset is only moderate: unrolled gas y-velocity errors are roughly 43–46%, volume-fraction errors are roughly 16–20%, and mean correlation times are around 60% of the trajectory. The practical consequences of these errors are not sufficiently analyzed.

Generalization evidence is narrow: there are only two two-dimensional datasets generated by the same CFD code, with small test sets of 9–10 cases. The split construction and whether evaluation parameters test interpolation or extrapolation are insufficiently characterized.

The framework predicts coarsened intervals obtained by aggregating hundreds of classical adaptive steps, rather than a timestep with an explicit learned stability or error-control guarantee. Calling this component a neural CFL model somewhat overstates its relationship to the classical CFL condition.

Overall, the work is promising and technically plausible, but the missing uniform-step, oracle-timestep, and efficiency baselines leave its main practical advantage insufficiently demonstrated for acceptance at a selective top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: learned surrogate modeling of compressible, shock-dominated flows on adaptive temporal grids.
The two-stage design—predicting a coarse timestep and then advancing a timestep-conditioned neural solver—is intuitive and practically motivated.
Evaluation spans several challenging configurations, including multiphase explosions, circular and spherical blasts, irregular airfoil geometry, and limited hypersonic and long-rollout studies.

The appendix provides substantial implementation, CFD-generation, computational-cost, runtime, oracle-timestep, and conservation analysis. Multiple solver architectures and three training runs are considered.
Reported speedups over the high-fidelity CFD solver are large, and the circular-blast rollouts achieve strong correlation and moderate field errors.
weaknesses: The experiments do not establish the central claimed advantage of adaptive temporal training. There is no properly trained uniform-timestep baseline using the same architectures and computational budget, nor a comparison to related continuous-time or learned adaptive-step methods. Replacing the neural CFL model with a mean timestep at inference creates out-of-distribution state–timestep pairs and is not a valid substitute for such a baseline.

There is no solver ablation without timestep conditioning. Because each state is observed with essentially one timestep and the timestep is highly predictable from the state, the solver may ignore the explicit timestep input. Consequently, the necessity and benefit of the proposed conditioning mechanisms are not demonstrated; Euler and MoE conditioning also yield small, inconsistent, or negative improvements.

The so-called neural CFL target is the accumulated duration of 100–500 adaptive CFD microsteps, not the classical one-step CFL limit and potentially depends on future states. The paper does not analyze this non-Markov target or clarify what physical stability property the learned predictor retains.

Performance is uneven in the harder regimes. Coal-dust rollouts have roughly 16% mean error, about 43–45% error for one velocity component, and only about 60% mean correlation duration. On this dataset ShockCast is approximately 9–17 correlation-percentage points below the ground-truth-timestep oracle, contradicting the characterization that it is close to the upper bound. Long-rollout errors rise to roughly 0.4–0.7 and correlation persists for only about half the trajectory.

The hypersonic evidence is only qualitative for a selected held-out case, excludes the difficult transverse-velocity field, and shows instantaneous relative errors as high as about 25%; it therefore does not substantiate general hypersonic capability.

Physical validation is limited to mass conservation for one closed-domain dataset. There is no systematic assessment of momentum/energy conservation, positivity, shock position and strength, entropy behavior, or stability under out-of-distribution Mach numbers and geometries.

Evaluation sets contain only 9–10 parameter-selected trajectories per principal dataset and mainly test interpolation within the training parameter ranges. This is weak evidence for generalization, especially given the large models and closely related trajectories.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence: the proposed conditioning methods are described as effective despite inconsistent gains, and stable-looking long rollouts are emphasized despite large quantitative errors. There are also presentation inconsistencies, including an incorrect dataset reference in the caption of Table 6.

strengths: The problem—efficient surrogate modeling of compressible, shock-dominated flows on adaptive temporal grids—is important and comparatively underexplored.
ShockCast is conceptually simple: a learned timestep predictor is coupled to a timestep-conditioned neural solver, with physically motivated timestep features and several conditioning mechanisms.

The empirical scope is broad, covering multiphase explosions, circular and spherical blasts, irregular airfoil geometry, longer rollouts, and multiple solver backbones. Runtime, conservation, oracle-timestep, and feature-importance analyses add useful context.
The manuscript is generally clear, and most figures and tables are well presented. The CFD generation procedure and many training details are documented.
weaknesses: The central motivation is not demonstrated experimentally. There is no controlled comparison against a neural solver trained on a uniform temporal grid at matched data, rollout-step, accuracy, and compute budgets. Comparing the neural CFL module with a constant mean timestep does not answer whether adaptive training is beneficial, since that constant produces state–timestep pairs outside the training distribution.

The learned timestep target is simply the accumulated interval obtained by retaining every J-th adaptive CFD step. Its optimality for the coarse neural solver is neither established nor learned; it inherits choices made for the fine classical discretization. Thus, the method primarily imitates a particular data-saving schedule rather than deriving an accuracy–cost-adaptive neural integrator.

Comparisons with prior variable-time or continuous-time neural solvers are absent. The experiments mainly compare backbones and the authors' own conditioning variants, so the paper does not establish competitiveness with relevant approaches discussed in the related-work section.

The proposed Euler and MoE conditioning mechanisms provide small, inconsistent gains. Affine conditioning is frequently best, while the MoE comparisons are confounded by substantially different parameter counts, memory, and computation—for example, the CNO MoE variant is roughly four times larger than its affine counterpart.

Several reported results are weak. Coal-dust rollout error for the y-velocity is about 43–45%, its correlation-time proportion is near 0.2, and long-blast relative error grows to roughly 0.4–0.5 with correlation lasting only about half the trajectory. These outcomes conflict with the broad claims of effective and stable evolution.

The statement that ShockCast approaches the oracle-timestep upper bound is misleading for the coal-dust task: Table 6 shows absolute correlation-proportion gaps of roughly 0.09–0.17, and the y-velocity plot shows a particularly large deficit. The table caption also incorrectly refers to the circular-blast setting despite reporting coal-dust results.

Evidence for the 3D spherical and hypersonic settings is largely qualitative. Dataset sizes, splits, repeated-run statistics, and comprehensive metrics are missing; the hypersonic experiment removes the difficult y-velocity field, further weakening the claimed extension.

Evaluation sets contain only 9–10 trajectories, and most conclusions are based on interpolation within narrow parameterized families generated by one CFD code. There is no out-of-range generalization, cross-resolution evaluation, robustness analysis for timestep errors, or systematic positivity and conservation assessment.

The runtime comparison uses only one circular-blast case and does not fully control hardware or compare end-to-end accuracy–cost tradeoffs across test cases. Training and dataset-generation costs are also omitted.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted PDF: the abstract's dataset/code availability sentence contains blank placeholders, and exact public artifacts, full configurations, and spherical/hypersonic training details are not supplied. The broader-impact discussion acknowledges dual-use applications but offers little concrete risk analysis or mitigation.

strengths: ShockCast addresses an important and comparatively underexplored problem: learned simulation of compressible, shock-dominated flows on adaptive temporal meshes. Predicting the timestep from the evolving state and conditioning the neural solver on that prediction is a clear, practically motivated contribution.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. The paper introduces substantial CFD data spanning multiphase coal-dust explosions, circular and spherical blasts, and shock-airfoil interactions, including regular and irregular geometries and a limited hypersonic extension.

The evaluation covers multiple solver families (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver, MGN, and DGN), several timestep-conditioning mechanisms, autoregressive rollouts, physical summary quantities, conservation behavior, computational cost, and comparison with oracle and constant-timestep predictors.

The neural-CFL studies provide useful evidence: physically motivated features help on the more complicated multiphase problem, predicted timesteps track the reference trajectories, and the learned predictor substantially outperforms simply using the training-set mean timestep.

The reported rollout results are encouraging, particularly the roughly 98% correlation-time proportion on circular blasts, stable rollouts exceeding 100 steps, and mass deviation below 0.2% in the closed circular-blast setting.

Runtime reporting is comparatively careful for neural PDE work: it includes CPU and GPU inference, parameter/FLOP/memory information, high- and low-fidelity classical comparisons, and large measured speedups.

The manuscript is technically detailed and generally reproducible, with extensive descriptions of CFD generation, grid-independence checks, model hyperparameters, training procedures, dataset splits, and uncertainty across three training runs. It also appropriately acknowledges stability and safety limitations for high-consequence applications.
weaknesses: The central claim that adaptive temporal meshes benefit neural solvers is not directly established. There is no controlled comparison against training and rolling out an otherwise identical solver on uniformly sampled trajectories, nor a matched-compute fixed-step baseline. Comparing learned timesteps only with the mean training timestep conflates adaptivity with severe state-timestep distribution shift.

The conditioning innovations provide inconsistent or very small gains. Affine conditioning is frequently as good as or better than Euler or MoE conditioning, and the preferred variant changes across metrics and datasets. Given the added cost—especially for dense MoE—the paper does not demonstrate a robust new conditioning method.

The neural-CFL oracle gap is substantial on the coal-dust problem: Table 6 indicates that ShockCast trails ground-truth-timestep conditioning by about 9–17 correlation-percentage points, which is difficult to reconcile with the text's claim that performance is close to the oracle upper bound. The table caption also incorrectly refers to the circular-blast setting.

Several claimed extensions are not evaluated with the rigor of the main 2D experiments. The spherical-blast and hypersonic-airfoil results are primarily qualitative; the latter changes architecture, interpolates to a regular grid, fixes angle of attack, and omits the difficult transverse-velocity field. These experiments therefore provide limited evidence of general 3D or hypersonic capability.

Evaluation sets contain only 9–10 trajectories per principal dataset, selected within the sampled parameter ranges. There is little evidence about extrapolation to stronger shocks, unseen geometries, different resolutions, different CFL policies, or substantially longer physical horizons.

The method imitates the classical solver's coarsened timestep sequence rather than learning an accuracy/cost controller or enforcing an error tolerance. Consequently, it has no explicit mechanism to reject unsafe steps, recover after rollout drift, or provide the reliability guarantees normally associated with adaptive integrators.

Physical validation is limited. Mass conservation is checked only for the simplest closed blast case, while positivity, momentum and energy conservation, shock location/strength, lift/drag, and other application-relevant quantities are not systematically assessed.

The experiments do not compare against the closest continuous-time or adaptive-time learned-solver alternatives discussed in related work. Even if those methods require adaptation to these data, a focused comparison would better establish the advantage of the proposed two-phase design.

Some presentation choices overstate the evidence: the paper describes three new datasets but also adds multiple extensions without consistently reporting their sizes or quantitative results, and the strongest high-speed-flow claims rest mostly on in-distribution interpolation over narrowly parameterized simulation families.
